analysis.one_liner: Bans federal oil and gas drilling permits within 1,500 feet of homes, schools, and businesses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Mineral Leasing Act, the law governing drilling on federal lands, to bar the Interior Department from approving any oil and gas drilling operation within 1,500 feet of a home, business, school, or other building needing special protection. The point was to keep drilling noise, truck traffic, and pollution away from the places people live, learn, and work. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or attend school near federal oil and gas drilling sites. A 1,500-foot buffer would reduce their exposure to drilling-related noise, heavy truck traffic, dust, and air emissions, and lower risks from accidents or leaks close to occupied buildings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near federal drilling sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the Interior Department from issuing a permit for any oil and gas drilling operation located within 1,500 feet of a home, business, school, or other building that requires special protection [S2] [S3].

The buffer is added directly to the Mineral Leasing Act, the statute governing oil and gas development on federal lands, so the protection becomes a standing rule rather than a case-by-case judgment [S3].
The Secretary of the Interior retains authority to determine which additional buildings qualify as requiring special protection [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies with federal leases near occupied buildings, which would lose the ability to drill within 1,500 feet of homes, schools, and businesses, potentially forgoing some recoverable oil and gas and the royalties and lease revenue tied to it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

drawbacks.text: The 1,500-foot buffer applies no matter how the land is used: drilling that would be far from any person in a rural area but slightly over the line from an isolated outbuilding would be barred alongside drilling next to a school, which could block some development with little health benefit.

Restricting where federal drilling can occur can reduce domestic oil and gas production, potentially raising costs for consumers and reducing federal royalty revenue in areas where the buffer applies.
An occupied-building setback alone does not address drilling pollution that drifts beyond 1,500 feet, so people slightly outside the buffer would get no protection from the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who live or study near federal drilling operations, a 1,500-foot setback is a meaningful health and safety protection, and setback rules of this kind are already used by many state and local governments. The costs fall on a specific industry and on federal mineral revenue, and the bill's one-size distance rule is blunt. On balance the benefits run to ordinary residents while the costs run to drillers, but the bill was so narrowly drafted — covering only Interior Department permits under the Mineral Leasing Act — that its practical reach is limited to federal leases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee in February 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Nanette Barragan introduced the bill on February 25, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1] [S5].
On March 8, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which is the last recorded action in the Congress [S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drillers on federal land keep the ability to seek permits near homes, schools, and businesses; residents near those sites get no new buffer protection.

for.name: Rep. Nanette Diaz Barragan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a 1,500-foot drilling buffer around homes, schools, and businesses.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Federal-lease drillers whose operations near occupied buildings the bill would have restricted
against.what_they_did: No group is recorded in the congressional record as acting on this bill; the bill generated no cosponsors and no recorded committee activity.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only one Democratic sponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers on federal land
industries.note: The bill would have barred Interior from issuing drilling permits within 1,500 feet of homes, schools, and businesses on federal leases, blocking development close to occupied buildings. Its failure leaves those operators free to seek permits next to residences.

Residents, students, and workers near federal drilling operations would have gained a fixed buffer from drilling noise, traffic, and emissions. The bill's death means no federal setback protection was added.
